     1	# #1608 — Phase 4c cold-path hardening — research plan **v3 (research-only)**
     2	
     3	> **History:** v1 PLAN-KILLED 2026-05-27 (6 fatal axes), v2 PLAN-KILLED
     4	> 2026-05-27 (10 new fatals), then PARKED pending #1606 + #1607 v2 + #1609.
     5	> This is the `/research` re-evaluation now that all three gating issues
     6	> are CLOSED. The deliverable is a converged 3-way plan (Codex + AGY +
     7	> Claude SMR) ending at PLAN-READY **or** PLAN-KILL. No PR, no production
     8	> code. See the v1/v2 kill comments on #1608 for the prior fatal lists;
     9	> they are not re-litigated here except where the landscape changed.
    10	
    11	## Section 1 — Problem statement & scope
    12	
    13	#1608 proposes two independent defensive mechanisms in front of the
    14	cold path (flow-cache miss → policy linear scan → session install):
    15	
    16	- **4c.1** per-source ingress rate-limit (token bucket before policy
    17	  eval) to bound cold-path work under a cold-flow flood.
    18	- **4c.2** verdict micro-cache keyed on the policy-match tuple to skip
    19	  re-running the full scan for repeated cold verdicts.
    20	
    21	This research asks the prior-to-design question the two PLAN-KILLs and
    22	the parking decision deferred: **is the cold path a measured bottleneck
    23	on the supported hardware, and do these two mechanisms add value that
    24	the merged #1606 (address-book dedup) + #1660 (dead-host negative
    25	cache) + #1620/#1635 (cold-path latency instrumentation) do not already
    26	provide?**
    27	
    28	## Section 2 — Current cold-path topology (verified against origin/master @ 6bdf9d73e)
    29	
    30	The cold path for a forwarded transit packet that misses the flow cache:
    31	
    32	1. `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:2392` `ForwardingDisposition::MissingNeighbor`
    33	   arm — **#1660 dead-host negative-cache gate fires FIRST**
    34	   (`neg_neigh_gate`, `:2418`). A negatively-cached, unresolved,
    35	   un-expired dst is recycled immediately: no probe, no `pending_neigh`
    36	   slot, no `MissingNeighborSeed` session, **no policy eval**.
    37	2. `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:1393` `evaluate_policy_result_with_len`
    38	   (ForwardCandidate slow path) — the canonical "policy decision on a
    39	   new flow". **Wrapped by the #1620/#1635 cold-path latency histogram**
    40	   (`cp_sample_tag`/`sample_tsc_start`/`record_sample`, `:1380-1445`).
    41	3. `poll_descriptor/mod.rs:2522` `evaluate_policy_with_len`
    42	   (session-install slow path; sessionless / NAT-driven forwarding).
    43	4. `policy.rs:873` `evaluate_policy_result_with_len`:
    44	   - `zone_pair_index.get(key)` — O(1) hash on `(from_zone, to_zone)`.
    45	   - `for &idx in indices` — **linear scan over that zone-pair's rule
    46	     indices** (`policy.rs:886`), then global indices (`:901`).
    47	   - `try_match_rule` (`policy.rs:926`): inactive gate → `compiled_apps`
    48	     O(1) protocol/port match → **`source_v4_match_any ||
    49	     source_literal_v4.contains() || source_book_idxs.iter().any(|i|
    50	     state.books[i].v4.contains())`** (`:944-949`).
    51	
    52	**Landscape change since v2 was planned (#1606 landed):** the per-rule
    53	address match is no longer "each rule independently builds its own
    54	PrefixSet of literal CIDRs." It is now: match-any short-circuit flag →
    55	per-rule literal `PrefixSetV4` (trie) → shared `state.books[idx]` dense
    56	address-book entries via `source_book_idxs`. Address-book bodies are
    57	deduplicated across rules (the #1605 1.6 TB memory blocker is gone). The
    58	remaining rule-count-linear cost is the **outer `for &idx in indices`
    59	zone-pair scan**, not the per-rule address set.
    60	
    61	**#1623 scaffolding landed but the DAG did NOT.** `PolicyRule` now
    62	carries `source_prefixes_v{4,6}: Option<Arc<[Prefix]>>` parallel arrays
    63	(`policy.rs:182-185`) for a *future* Multi-Book LPM builder, but the
    64	multi-stage DAG (#1609 → #1623) was PLAN-KILLED after 6 rounds. The
    65	production cold path is **still the linear zone-pair scan**.
    66	
    67	## Section 3 — The measurement gap (load-bearing for the whole issue)
    68	
    69	#1608's own acceptance criteria are CPU-percentage and cycle-count
    70	deltas under synthetic floods. The prerequisite that was supposed to
    71	supply the baseline — #1607/#1611/#1612 hardware-ceiling measurement —
    72	**did not produce a populated Scale Target table.** Verified:
    73	`docs/userspace-jit-design.md` has a "Measurement plan" section but
    74	**zero populated A1/A2/B1/B2 rows** (grep: no `p50`/`p99`/`ns/packet`
    75	table). #1612's closing comment states the flooder capped at **~870 K
    76	pps** (container IPVLAN/virtio TX ceiling, #1615), which is **~145 K
    77	pps/worker** across 6 workers — *far below* the ~5 Mpps/worker cold-path
    78	saturation observed in smoke baselines. **The cold path was never driven
    79	to saturation on this hardware, so its per-packet cost and its position
    80	on the bottleneck frontier are unmeasured.**
    81	
    82	The #1605 kill verdict already quantified the established-flow side:
    83	JIT-the-rewrite saves 0.4-0.6% of one core because the dominant costs
    84	are memcpy (8%), NAPI (12%), syscalls (3%), poll_binding (22%). No
    85	equivalent flamegraph exists for the *cold* path under flood. The only
    86	in-tree cold-path instrument is the #1620/#1635 latency histogram, which
    87	measures *latency per cold eval*, not *fraction of a core under flood*.
    88	
    89	**Hostile framing:** absent a measured cold-path saturation profile,
    90	both mechanisms are defending a threat model that has not been
    91	demonstrated on the supported dataplane. The burden of this plan is to
    92	either (a) cite a real measurement, or (b) justify the mechanisms as
    93	pure availability defense-in-depth with a bounded, near-zero steady-state
    94	cost — and show they are not already covered by #1660.
    95	
    96	## Section 4 — Overlap analysis vs #1660 (dead-host negative cache)
    97	
    98	#1660 (merged, `neg_neigh.rs`) already fast-fails one of the three
    99	attack classes #1608 names:
   100	
   101	| #1608 attack class | Reaches policy eval today? | Covered by #1660? |
   102	|---|---|---|
   103	| SYN flood, random src IP, **dead/unresolved dst** | NO — `neg_neigh_gate` recycles before policy eval after the first per-dst probe times out | **YES** (per-dst, per-binding, 3 s TTL) |
   104	| SYN flood, random src IP, **live/on-link dst** (the firewall's own subnets) | YES — resolves, hits policy eval every packet | NO |
   105	| Port scan, single src, sweeping dport, **live dst** | YES — policy eval per packet | NO |
   106	| DNS amplification inbound, source-spoofed, **live dst** | YES — policy eval per packet | NO |
   107	
   108	So #1608 is NOT a duplicate of #1660, but its *most-cited* example
   109	(SYN flood to random/dead hosts) is already handled. The residual
   110	threat #1608 uniquely addresses is **flood to a LIVE, resolvable dst**
   111	(the victim service or the firewall's own interface) where every packet
   112	legitimately reaches policy eval. This narrows the real scope
   113	considerably and must be stated honestly.
   114	
   115	## Section 5 — Why v1 and v2 died (carried forward, must not regress)
   116	
   117	Convergent fatals the v3 design space inherits as hard constraints:
   118	
   119	- **4c.1 keying physics.** AF_XDP RSS sprays the 5-tuple across N
   120	  workers; a per-worker per-source-IP bucket sees ~1/N of an attacker.
   121	  v2's per-DESTINATION key is the only worker-local key that sees the
   122	  full share of a flood (the victim dst is RSS-invariant within a
   123	  worker's queue share). Any v3 MUST use a per-worker honest semantic
   124	  with documented N multiplier OR pay cross-worker MESI (killed).
   125	- **4c.1 must drop SILENTLY** outside the policy engine: counter +
   126	  `scratch_recycle` + `continue`, NO `emit_policy_deny_event` (v2 fatal
   127	  #1 — per-packet event stream is itself a DoS), and the drop must
   128	  actually `continue` (v2 fatal #2 — a non-Permit return at `:2522`
   129	  fell through to session install).
   130	- **4c.1 bucket init must be zero/single-packet credit, not full
   131	  burst** (v2 fatal #3 — eviction storm grants a fresh burst per miss).
   132	- **4c.1 bucket key must include zone/profile** (v2 fatal #4 — Junos
   133	  screen profiles are per-zone).
   134	- **4c.1 refill must be fixed-point or consumed-ns** (v1 fatal #4 —
   135	  `elapsed_ns × pps / 1e9` truncates to 0 under fast polling, permanent
   136	  DoS).
   137	- **4c.2 cache MUST cache `policy_id == 0` (default-deny)** (v2 fatal #5
   138	  — the typical flood is no-match → default-deny; skipping it = 0% hit
   139	  under the exact attack). Rely on `config_generation` for safety.
   140	- **4c.2 key MUST cover every `try_match_rule` input** (from/to zone
   141	  IDs, src/dst IP, protocol, src/dst port) AND carry a #1431-style
   142	  CACHE-KEY INVARIANT comment block on `PolicyRule` — NOT a
   143	  `mem::size_of` proxy (v2 fatal #9 — `Vec`/`Arc`/`String` fields make
   144	  size invariant to semantic additions; the #1623 `Option<Arc<[T]>>`
   145	  fields prove the struct grows without `size_of` catching match-dim
   146	  changes).
   147	- **Storage: per-worker (not per-binding) ownership; `size_of` proofs**
   148	  (v2 fatals #6, #7 — const_assert sizes were wrong, ownership boundary
   149	  blew the L2 budget).
   150	- **Acceptance can't be a single-thread cargo bench** (v1 fatal #6 /
   151	  v2 fatal — must gate on a wire-line harness or downgrade to cycle
   152	  counts; the #1607 harness is still TX-capped per #1615).
   153	
   154	## Section 6 — Multiple Path Options
   155	
   156	### Path A — PLAN-KILL (recommended default unless measurement appears)
   157	
   158	Close-with-rationale. Rationale:
   159	1. The cold-path bottleneck is **unmeasured** on supported hardware
   160	   (Section 3); #1607/#1612 never populated the Scale Target table and
   161	   #1615 still caps the only flooder at 870 K pps.
   162	2. The most-cited attack (flood to dead/random dst) is **already
   163	   handled by #1660** (Section 4).
   164	3. The residual threat (flood to a *live* dst reaching policy eval) is a
   165	   genuine availability concern but is **not demonstrated** to saturate
   166	   a worker at realistic rule counts: post-#1606 the per-rule cost is a
   167	   match-any flag + a trie `contains` + a shared-book `contains`, and
   168	   the rule-count-linear part is the zone-pair index scan — which #1609's
   169	   DAG was the chartered fix for (killed, but the cost was never shown to
   170	   bite in production).
   171	4. Both v1 and v2 died on structural fatals; the design surface is
   172	   demonstrably deep, and there is no measured win to justify the risk.
   173	
   174	PLAN-KILL leaves the issue OPEN with `plan-kill`, preserving the v3
   175	research so a future author with a real measurement can resurrect it.
   176	
   177	### Path B — 4c.2 verdict micro-cache ONLY, gated on a measured win
   178	
   179	Ship the verdict cache against the existing linear scan, deferring 4c.1
   180	entirely. Justified ONLY if a measurement (Path D first) shows the
   181	zone-pair linear scan is a real cold-path cost at the operator's rule
   182	count. Design constraints (all from Section 5): full policy-tuple key
   183	incl. both zone IDs; cache default-deny; `config_generation` stamp for
   184	invalidation; #1431-style CACHE-KEY INVARIANT comment on `PolicyRule`;
   185	per-worker set-associative table (e.g. 2-way × 2 K = 4 K entries) with
   186	real `size_of` proof ≤ budget; insertion at the `policy.rs:873` site or
   187	immediately wrapping the two call sites (`:1393`, `:2522`). Correctness
   188	hazard: staleness across config reload — must invalidate on
   189	`config_generation` bump, which is already the flow-cache invalidation
   190	primitive.
   191	
   192	### Path C — 4c.1 silent per-destination rate-limit ONLY
   193	
   194	Ship the rate-limit against live-dst floods only, deferring 4c.2. All
   195	Section-5 4c.1 constraints apply. This is the only mechanism that adds
   196	something #1660 does not (live-dst floods). Default-off, per-zone knob,
   197	per-worker bucket with documented N multiplier, zero-credit init,
   198	fixed-point refill, silent drop. Hostile concern: interaction with the
   199	**legitimate-burst** case (a real client opening many short-lived
   200	connections, e.g. a web crawler or a CDN origin pull) — a per-dst bucket
   201	on the firewall's own service IP would throttle legitimate cold connects;
   202	must be default-off and documented as an attack-mitigation knob, not a
   203	general policy.
   204	
   205	### Path D — Measurement-first (precondition for B or C)
   206	
   207	Do NOT ship either mechanism until a cold-path saturation profile exists
   208	on real hardware. This means resolving #1615 (flooder TX ceiling) OR
   209	running the flooder from a non-container source that can push >2.5 Mpps,
   210	then populating the Scale Target table. Only then is the bottleneck
   211	claim falsifiable and the acceptance criteria meetable. This is the
   212	honest precondition the v2 kill and the parking decision both gestured
   213	at; it has not been satisfied.
   214	
   215	### Recommendation
   216	
   217	**Path A (PLAN-KILL) as the default**, with Path D as the documented
   218	reopen criterion. The two gating issues that were supposed to make a v3
   219	"narrow" (#1607 measurement, #1609 DAG) both failed to deliver their
   220	deliverable — the measurement is still absent and the DAG never shipped.
   221	The mechanisms therefore still sit in front of an unmeasured cold path,
   222	and the strongest attack example is already covered by #1660. If a
   223	future measurement shows the live-dst flood saturates a worker, Path C
   224	(rate-limit only) is the higher-value reopen; Path B (verdict cache) is
   225	second and depends on rule-count-linear scan cost being demonstrated.
   226	
   227	## Section 7 — Hot-path cost (steady state) for B and C
   228	
   229	Both mechanisms claim near-zero steady-state cost. Verified concerns:
   230	- 4c.1: one hash lookup + token check per **cold** packet only (the hot
   231	  flow-cache-hit path is untouched). But a per-dst hash on every cold
   232	  packet competes for the same L1/L2 lines as the policy scan it
   233	  precedes; under benign cold traffic (legit new connects) it is pure
   234	  overhead. Must be default-off.
   235	- 4c.2: one hash lookup per cold packet; on a hit it skips the scan. Net
   236	  win only if (scan cost − cache lookup cost) × hit rate > miss-path
   237	  insert cost. Unquantified without Path D.
   238	
   239	## Section 8 — Memory bounds
   240	
   241	Per-worker, not per-binding (v2 fatal #7). With corrected Rust layout
   242	(v2 established `TokenBucket`=32 B, `DestBucketEntry`=56 B,
   243	`VerdictCacheEntry`=96 B): a 4 K-entry verdict cache alone is ~384 KB,
   244	already over the 256 KB issue budget. Path B must either halve entries
   245	(2 K × 96 B = 192 KB) or split v4/v6 tables. Path C's per-dst bucket
   246	table at 56 B × 2 K = 112 KB. Combined exceeds 256 KB → the issue's own
   247	memory acceptance criterion is unmeetable at 4 K entries; must be
   248	re-derived if B or C proceeds.
   249	
   250	## Section 9 — Correctness hazards (B and C)
   251	
   252	- **Verdict-cache staleness across config reload (B):** a cached permit
   253	  for a rule that a commit just deleted must not be honored. Mitigation:
   254	  `config_generation` stamp in the key or a generation field compared on
   255	  hit, evicting on mismatch. This is the same primitive the flow cache
   256	  uses; the hazard is real but solved if the stamp is mandatory.
   257	- **Verdict-cache match-dimension drift (B):** any future `PolicyRule`
   258	  match dimension (time-of-day via `scheduler_name`, already a field at
   259	  `policy.rs:128`; or a new DSCP/flag match) silently corrupts cached
   260	  verdicts. The `mem::size_of` proxy does NOT catch this. A #1431-style

    89	## Motivation
    90	
    91	The userspace AF_XDP dataplane currently interprets every packet through a
    92	generic pipeline: parse metadata, screen, session lookup, policy evaluation,
    93	NAT decision, FIB lookup, frame rewrite. For established flows (>99% of
    94	transit packets), the session-hit path still executes ~15 branches and 3-4
    95	hash map lookups that always produce the same answer.
    96	
    97	The eBPF dataplane avoids this with a per-CPU flow cache (`xdp_zone.c`) that
    98	stores the complete forwarding decision (egress ifindex, MACs, NAT flags,
    99	policy ID) and replays it in O(1) for subsequent packets in the same flow.
   100	The userspace dataplane has no equivalent.
   101	
   102	A JIT compiler can close this gap by generating specialized machine code for
   103	the common-case packet paths, eliminating branches, hash lookups, and
   104	indirection that the interpreter must execute on every packet.
   105	
   106	## What the eBPF pipeline precomputes that userspace doesn't
   107	
   108	| Feature | eBPF (compile-time) | Userspace (per-packet) |
   109	|---------|---------------------|----------------------|
   110	| Zone lookup | `iface_zone_map` HASH: O(1) | Same: O(1) HashMap |
   111	| Address matching | LPM trie + membership HASH: O(log N) + O(1) | Linear scan of CIDR list |
   112	| Policy rules | Flat ARRAY indexed by `set_id * MAX + idx` | Linear scan of Vec |
   113	| Application match | HASH by `(proto, port)`: O(1) | Linear scan of application terms |
   114	| Flow cache | Per-CPU 256-slot array: O(1) established hit | None; full session lookup every packet |
   115	| Session lookup | Dual-entry HASH: O(1) forward+reverse | Multi-scope fallthrough with Mutex locks |
   116	| NAT pool alloc | Atomic per-CPU counter | Mutex-protected PortAllocator |
   117	| Frame rewrite | Inline in xdp_nat with incremental csum | Generic function with branch per NAT type |
   118	
   119	## Where a JIT wins
   120	
   121	### 1. Per-flow compiled fast-path (highest impact)
   122	
   123	When a session is created, the JIT compiles a small function that encodes
   124	the complete forwarding decision for that flow:
   125	
   126	```

   128	// Zone: trust -> wan, SNAT to 172.16.80.8, egress ge-0-0-2.80
   129	fn flow_0x7a3b(frame: &mut [u8]) -> TxTarget {
   130	    // Ethernet: fixed MACs + VLAN 80 (12 bytes, no branch)
   500	- Warm iperf3: 23+ Gbps (8 streams, 10s)
   501	- Fabric redirect iperf3: 16.9 Gbps (cross-chassis, 4 streams)
   502	- Warm ICMP: 0% loss, consistent TTL=63 (50 probes)
   503	- mtr IPv4/IPv6: intermediate hops visible (embedded ICMP NAT reversal)
   504	- Baseline before userspace dataplane: ~13 Gbps (eBPF kernel path)
   505	- Flow cache hit path (skipping session/policy/NAT/FIB) contributed
   506	  ~35% of the improvement; remaining gains from zero-copy XSK path
   507	
   508	**Files**:
   509	- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp.rs` — flow cache, `compute_ip_csum_delta()`,
   510	  `compute_l4_csum_delta()` (now handles IPv6), cache-hit wiring
   511	- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/frame.rs` — `apply_rewrite_descriptor()` with
   512	  6 unit tests (no-NAT, SNAT+VLAN, DNAT-VLAN, IPv6, port mismatch, NAT64 fallback)
   513	- `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/session_glue.rs` — descriptor construction
   514	
   515	**Test criteria**:
   516	- Established-flow throughput improves (measured by perf-compare)
   517	- `flow_cache_hits / total_packets > 0.9` for sustained TCP
   518	- No regression in HA failover tests
   519	- 6 unit tests validate checksum correctness for all NAT/VLAN combos
   520	
   521	### Phase 2: Policy decision trees — DONE
   522	
   523	**Scope**: Compile policies into zone-pair decision functions at
   524	config apply time.
   525	
   526	1. In `buildPolicySnapshots()`, generate a decision tree representation
   527	2. Pass decision tree to Rust helper as part of ConfigSnapshot
   528	3. In Rust, compile decision tree into a match cascade
   529	4. On session miss, call zone-pair decision function instead of
   530	   linear policy scan
   531	
   532	**Expected gain**: O(1)-O(log N) policy evaluation vs O(N) linear scan.
   533	Significant for rulesets with 20+ rules per zone-pair.
   534	
   535	### Phase 3: Address-book trie compilation — WIRE FORMAT LANDED (#1606), TRIE COMPACTION DEFERRED TO #1608
   536	
   537	**Wire format (done in #1606)**: ConfigSnapshot now carries a top-
   538	level `address_books: Vec<AddressBookSnapshot>` table. Multiple
   539	named books with identical canonical CIDR content share one row
   540	and one u32 ID (content-hashed). Each `PolicyRuleSnapshot` cites
   541	books by ID via `source_book_ids` / `destination_book_ids` and
   542	free-form CIDRs via `source_literals` / `destination_literals`.
   543	The legacy `source_addresses` field stays on the wire for one-
   544	release rolling-upgrade compatibility with old Rust binaries.
   545	
   546	The Rust side stores books in a flat dense `Vec<BookEntry>` on
   547	`PolicyState`; rules carry `SmallVec<[u32; 8]>` indices. No
   548	`Arc<BookEntry>` per rule; the table lifetime is tied to the
   549	ArcSwap-published `ForwardingState` snapshot.
   550	
   551	This delivers the **structural memory deduplication** prerequisite
   552	for the 1M-policy scale: prefix-table memory is now
   553	`O(book_count × per_book_size)` not
   554	`O(rule_count × avg_books_per_rule)`. A 10K-book × 100K-rule
   555	config with 3 books per rule averages 30× fewer prefix-set
   556	materializations than today.
   557	
   558	**Trie compaction (deferred to #1608)**: the per-book `PrefixSetV4`/
   559	`PrefixSetV6` is still the uncompressed binary trie introduced in
   560	#923. At 10K books × 1K CIDRs each, that's ~25 GB of trie node
   561	memory — usable but not optimal. #1608 will replace the binary
   562	trie with a DIR-24-8 or Patricia compressed structure to bring
   563	the per-book footprint down 10-100×.
   564	
   565	### Phase 4: Cranelift JIT for flow rewrite functions — NOT STARTED
   566	
   567	**Scope**: Replace rewrite descriptors with native code generation.
   568	
   569	1. Add Cranelift dependency
   570	2. At session creation, emit Cranelift IR for the rewrite function

docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:27:Explanation: The plan first states that 25 Gbps line rate is about 2.08 Mpps “per queue,” then immediately divides that by 16 workers to create a 130 Kpps and 7600 ns “per-packet CPU budget” (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:240-247`). docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:14:1. **Proportional Mode Divergence (Major):** Running the A1.1 allocator on the default `fraction = 0.0` mode is *not* bit-for-bit identical to the current scheduler. docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:24:### A. §4 A1.1 Algorithm Walk and Regression Evaluation
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:25:We walked the proposed A1.1 two-phase algorithm at fractions $0.0$, $0.4$, $0.7$, and $1.0$ under the $109/18$ oversubscription fixture (aggregate capacity $C = 18\text{ G}$):
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:46:If the A1.1 allocator is executed for all values of `pass1_guarantee_fraction`, the following deviations occur:
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:47:1.  **Starvation of Equal-Rate Queues:** The current scheduler uses a round-robin cursor `exact_guarantee_rr` (`queue_service/mod.rs:600-602`) that advances per selection. The A1.1 allocator instead iterates over a *fixed* ascending order `root.exact_queues_by_rate_ascending`. If there are multiple exact queues with the same configured rate (e.g., two `3g` classes), the queue that appears first in the precomputed sorted vector will *always* be preferred, starving the second queue during saturation.
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:48:2.  **Budget Scaling Perturbation:** The current scheduler select-drains exactly $Q_i = \text{quantum}_i$. Under A1.1, the budget allocated per visit is scaled dynamically to $\text{cap} \times Q_i / \sum Q_{\text{unhonored}}$, which alters the size of the drain quantum depending on token fullness and active queue counts.
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:50:**Required Structural Fix:** The scheduler must **explicitly branch**. If `oversubscription-policy` is `proportional` (or `fraction == 0.0`), the scheduler must bypass the A1 allocator code entirely and execute the legacy `select_exact_cos_guarantee_queue_with_lease_telemetry` round-robin selection block.
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:59:If the `loss:cluster-userspace-host` 16-CPU virtio container is physically bound by generator CPU interrupts, softirqs, or virtio-NET segmentation during push runs, implementing a two-phase allocator will not raise the aggregate firewall throughput above 18 G. Moving the R8 sanity check (parallel 11-stream reverse direction run, aggregate $\ge 22\text{ G}$) to **Phase 0 (blocking, before A1 implementation)** is a vital defensive gate that prevents wasted implementation hours on a bottlenecked generator test-bed.
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:88:**Required Structural Fix:** The priority-low min-share must be calculated **before** the A1 allocator runs. The scheduler should subtract the priority-low min-share from the overall pass capacity `cap`:
docs/pr/1614-multi-rss-cos/agy-plan-r2.md:90:The A1 two-phase waterfill allocator should then execute on $\text{cap}_{\text{eff}}$. This ensures control-plane survivability is guaranteed under *all* oversubscription policies, including `proportional`.

docs/issues/issue-history.md:15863:I see `metadata.clone()` and `ingress_zone.clone()` called throughout the fast path in `afxdp.rs`. Every time you clone an `Arc`, the CPU executes a `LOCK XADD` instruction to atomically increment the refcount. This instruction forces a cache coherency message to all other cores, stalling the pipeline. At 14.8M pps, you are saturating the memory bus with atomic increments just to copy a string pointer.

docs/issues/issue-history.md:16747:If you have 1 million concurrent flows (a reasonable number for 100G), this O(N) sweep will freeze the worker thread for **several milliseconds** every time the GC interval hits. This is the definition of a 'Stop The World' latency spike. During this pause, the XSK RX rings will overflow, packets will be dropped, and hardware queues will stall. The tail latency (p99) of your firewall will be catastrophically bad.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:17595:A `thread_local!` access in Rust is not free. It compiles down to a TLS (Thread Local Storage) lookup, which can involve function calls (`__tls_get_addr`) depending on the linkage model. By putting this *inside* your 14.8M pps forwarding loop, you are adding hidden function calls and branch instructions to the most performance-critical code in the system. Even if gated by cold branches, the instruction footprint pollutes the L1-i cache.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:17642:Each `ArcSwap::load()` involves an atomic pointer load and an `Arc` refcount increment/decrement. At 14.8M pps, performing 8 separate loads per packet translates to hundreds of millions of atomic operations per second, saturating the memory bus interconnect (QPI/UPI) even without explicit locks.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:18222:2. **TCP RWND throttle on ACK egress** instead of ECN-mark/drop. Sender's cwnd is bounded by min(cwnd, swnd); reduce swnd to throttle leading flows. Industry-standard transparent-shaper technique (F5, A10). No receiver opt-in required. Sidesteps Gemini's ECN deployment-reality PLAN-KILL.

docs/pr/825-p3-tx-kick-latency/plan.md:234:Doc-comment invariant on `tx_kick_latency_hist`: `sum(tx_kick_latency_hist) ≈ tx_kick_latency_count` with bounded skew `|sum - count| ≤ K_skew`. **K_skew carries over from #812 §3.6 R2 as a conservative upper bound, not a re-derivation** (LOW-7 R1 clarification + R2 refinement): #812's K_skew=3 was derived from 3 Mpps completion rate at 1 µs read window. Kicks occur strictly less frequently than submits (each kick attempts to drain one or more submits), but the precise kick-per-packet rate is unmeasured pre-instrumentation and is workload-dependent (#823 showed worker on-CPU ~100%; wake cadence is gated by `TX_WAKE_MIN_INTERVAL_NS` at `tx.rs:6432-6434` but the effective rate under load is not directly known). Post-instrumentation, `tx_kick_latency_count` becomes the exact measure. Carrying #812's K_skew=3 bound is therefore a **deliberate conservative choice**: the bound that holds for the hotter submit-stamp path trivially holds for the strictly-rarer kick path, regardless of the unmeasured precise rate.

docs/issues/pr-history.md:7929:**Refill strategy: lazy per-bucket (strategy b in the brief), diverges from plan §4.** Plan §4 specified a single shared `pacing_last_refill_ns: u64` + O(1024) refill loop on every admission. At 1 Gbps × 83 kpps that's 83M u64 adds/second — pit-of-expensive. This PR lands per-bucket timestamps up front (8 KB extra per queue) to keep the hot path O(1). Plan §7 had deferred this to a follow-up; I'm landing it now because the perf cost otherwise is baked into every admission. Called out here honestly per engineering-style.md "trust but verify". If the reviewer disagrees, reverting to shared-timestamp is one array removal.

docs/issues/pr-history.md:24480:## PR #1533 — wg: document outer IPv4 UDP cs=0 default + add wire-byte regression gate (#1501 A2) [MERGED] (merged 2026-05-25)
docs/issues/pr-history.md:24492:Linux kernel WireGuard uses `udp_tunnel_xmit_skb(..., nocheck: false)` with `port4.use_udp_checksums = true` in `drivers/net/wireguard/socket.c` — the kernel computes the outer UDP cs on IPv4. The #1501 A2 issue body claim that "kernel WG does cs=0 for outer-IPv4 traffic" is factually wrong about kernel WG behavior. RFC 768 permits the choice; this engine takes it intentionally, accepting the known midbox-compat risk the integration layer can manage via an `outer-udp-checksum compute|zero` knob.

docs/userspace-dataplane-gaps.md:44:| Source NAT (pool mode) | Implemented with scoped caveats | IPv4/IPv6 pool address and port allocation. Global `source address-persistent` uses the documented userspace-v1 SHA-256 source-IP hash and is stable only within the AF_XDP backend, pool family, pool order, and pool size. Legacy eBPF uses C-word IPv4 modulo / IPv6 lane-XOR selection (DPDK retired #1525), so new-flow pool address parity is not promised across retained backend transitions. Pool-mode rules with missing pools, empty pools, invalid port ranges, malformed addresses, no address for the packet family, or exhausted live translated tuples fail-closed at the `poll_descriptor.rs` source-NAT call sites before session creation or forwarding, with recent-exception reasons such as `source_nat_pool_missing`, `source_nat_pool_empty`, `source_nat_pool_invalid_port_range`, and `source_nat_pool_exhausted`. Per-pool `persistent-nat` now has snapshot fields and runtime lease reuse keyed by source tuple `(protocol, source IP, source port)` to translated tuple. The lease table is bounded in helper memory, survives compatible in-process snapshot refreshes, and expires after the configured inactivity timeout once no live flow uses the lease. It does not consult Go `PersistentNATTable` and does not survive helper restart. The closed #1449 contract gates HA behavior explicitly: HA configs that reference persistent source-NAT pools are not admitted because leases are not synchronized, and status reports `userspace persistent-nat source pool leases are not HA-synchronized`. Userspace status, CLI summary, and Prometheus expose live-flow, used-port, persistent-lease, allocation, reuse, and exhaustion counters for admitted non-HA pools. |

docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:6:Explanation: The plan says the owner worker writes the histogram with `fetch_add(1, Relaxed)` and the control thread snapshots it with `load(Relaxed)`, explicitly mirroring the existing drain-histogram pattern (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:334-336`). Current code documents that pattern as intentionally tear-tolerant: `BindingLiveState::snapshot()` says bucket arrays are copied under `Relaxed`, read skew is acceptable, and even the existing `sum(hist) ≈ drain_invocations` relation only holds in steady-state (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem.rs:1322-1329`). The same plan then turns `sum(buckets) == tx_submit_latency_count` into both a merge-blocking invariant and an integration hard stop (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:341-346`, `docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:487-488`), which is not defensible under relaxed cross-CPU reads.
docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:18:Summary: The plan prices the submit timestamp as a 256-way amortized cost, but current TX code already has accepted-prefix/retry-tail behavior where the batch can be effectively size 1.
docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:20:Explanation: The design says one `monotonic_nanos()` call per submit commit is enough, and the cost table prices that as `15 ns / 256 = 0.06 ns` per packet (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:92-99`, `docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:208-217`). That is not a worst case: current `transmit_batch` and `transmit_prepared_batch` already support partial acceptance and explicitly peel the accepted prefix from the retry tail after `writer.commit()` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:5924-5960`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:6141-6175`). When `inserted == 1`, the submit clock read is per-packet, not amortized, so the advertised 1.1 ns submit subtotal is off by an order of magnitude.
docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:22:Mitigation: Budget the feature against observed batch-size distributions, and publish a worst-case small-batch number separately instead of passing a 256-descriptor best case off as the hot-path cost.
docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:27:Explanation: The plan first states that 25 Gbps line rate is about 2.08 Mpps “per queue,” then immediately divides that by 16 workers to create a 130 Kpps and 7600 ns “per-packet CPU budget” (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:240-247`). That is a load-distribution assumption, not a property of the queue being instrumented, so it is the wrong denominator for a per-packet hot-path claim. The same section counts one completion-side atomic (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:223-229`), but §12 later says the exact `tx_submit_latency_sum_ns` requires an additional `fetch_add(delta, Relaxed)` and asserts that cost is somehow already included in the bucket increment line (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:631-636`), which is plainly false.
docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:41:Explanation: Current offsets do come from UMEM frames and are aligned to the fixed frame size, so a dense index is structurally sound (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem.rs:21-27`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem.rs:76-82`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp.rs:147`). The problem is cardinality: the plan sizes the sidecar to `total_frames` and claims `8192 × 8 B = 64 KiB` per binding (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:180-192`), but virtio bindings actually use `3 × ring_entries` frames (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/bind.rs:37-43`) and `BindingWorker::new` uses that `total_frames` value when provisioning the binding (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker.rs:213-216`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker.rs:303`). The plan also dismisses cross-worker contention on the histogram while only later hinting at cacheline isolation in the estimate table (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:201-204`, `docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:496`; `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem.rs:168-180`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/umem.rs:186-190`).
docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:53:Summary: “Correct for 16 buckets” is not a valid decision rule when the proposed verdicts are shape tests across buckets, cells, and correlations.
docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:55:Explanation: The existing Step 1 methodology insists on named thresholds and explicitly justified investigation-level rules (`docs/pr/line-rate-investigation/step1-plan.md:1128-1135`). The new plan instead says that because the rerun adds 16 bucket counts per cell, a Bonferroni or equivalent correction should be applied over the 16 buckets before any D-subdivision fires (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:585-591`). But the same section defines D1/D2/D3 as multi-bucket shape patterns and cross-signal correlations, not 16 independent single-bucket nulls (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:561-581`), so the stated correction family is almost certainly the wrong one.

docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:69:Explanation: The architect explicitly says all six submit sites and the reap site should use `monotonic_nanos()` for the measured delta (`docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:74-77`, `docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/plan.md:101-111`), and the current helper is a single `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` implementation (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/neighbor.rs:3-15`). docs/pr/812-tx-latency-histogram/codex-plan-review.md:140:`2e6 × 1e-6 = 2.0`, so `ceil(2.0) = 2`; on the arithmetic alone, the revised `K_skew = 2` step is correct. The remaining problem is the rate premise: the same paragraph says 25 Gbps at 64B is about 48.8 Mpps aggregate, then about 12.2 Mpps across 4 workers, which is about 3.05 Mpps per worker, not 2 Mpps, so `λ = 2 Mpps` is not the conservative ceiling the text claims. If the intended upper bound is the plan's own small-packet line-rate case, the defensible bound is `λ ≈ 3 Mpps`, giving `K_skew = ceil(3e6 × 1e-6) = 3`. On the off-CPU gate, `4 ms × 2 Mpps = 8000` and `8000/200000 = 4%`, so a 1% gate would trip on a snapshot-thread preemption if the denominator were only a 77 ms accumulation window; that is scheduling jitter, not bucket-accounting corruption, so it would be a false positive in that short-window regime. The gate only makes sense as an integration-level check when `count` is the full long-run total, where a one-off 4 ms preemption is diluted well below 1%.

docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:1:# PR #796 Phase 3 MQFQ VFT — Adversarial Review
docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:8:`cos_queue_pop_front()` increments `queue.queue_vtime` immediately after removing the item (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4113-4119`). Every flow-fair retry path restores the item with `cos_queue_push_front()` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:2628-2630`, `2638-2647`, `2696-2699`, `2751-2753`, `5530-5552`), but `cos_queue_push_front()` repairs only `head_finish` and `flow_bucket_bytes`; it never rewinds `queue_vtime` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4089-4096`). Concrete case: flow A is popped during a TX-ring-full cycle and restored; `queue_vtime` becomes 1500 although zero bytes left the queue. A newly-idle flow B then enqueues at `max(0, 1500) + 1500 = 3000` via `account_cos_queue_flow_enqueue()` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:3914-3919`) instead of 1500, so B is artificially pushed behind established traffic. This also breaks the premise of the “100 Gbps x 46 years” headroom claim, because `queue_vtime` growth is no longer bounded by real drain rate.  
docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:12:`mqfq_push_front_is_finish_time_neutral_on_active_bucket()` captures `pre_pop_head`, `pre_pop_tail`, and `pre_pop_bytes`, then after restore checks only those fields (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:10730-10755`). The test comment says the round-trip must leave the queue in “the same state” (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:10688-10703`), but it never records or re-checks `queue_vtime`. On current code that omission is material: the test passes while the queue’s virtual time remains advanced by a packet that was not transmitted.  
docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:16:`mqfq_finish_time_u64_has_decades_of_headroom()` computes the wrap interval from local constants and a local `u64`, not from `CoSQueueRuntime.flow_bucket_head_finish_bytes`, `flow_bucket_tail_finish_bytes`, or `account_cos_queue_flow_enqueue()` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:10764-10782`). Narrowing the production fields, changing the actual delta applied per packet, or over-advancing `queue_vtime` would not necessarily fail this test. As written it proves the arithmetic in the test body, not that the rebased implementation still has 46-year headroom.  
docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:20:The `promote_cos_queue_flow_fair()` docblock still says the “current policy” is `flow_fair = queue.exact && !shared_exact` and tells reviewers to reject dropping the `!shared_exact` clause (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4924-4978`), but the implementation now sets `queue.flow_fair = queue.exact` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4990-5006`) and the new tests require shared_exact queues to be promoted (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:13217-13282`). Separately, `CoSQueueRuntime.queue_vtime` is documented as updating to the drained bucket’s finish (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types.rs:1088-1091`), while the code and its own new pin define it as `+= bytes_drained` (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4113-4119`, `10554-10606`). These are not runtime bugs today, but they are exactly the kind of stale invariant text that makes the next refactor regress back toward the wrong behavior.  
docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:25:The core byte-rate ordering logic is otherwise materially better than the old DRR path. Selection now scans `flow_bucket_head_finish_bytes` rather than ring position (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:3987-3997`), enqueue splits head and tail correctly (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:3894-3919`), non-drain pop advances head by the next head packet’s size (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4120-4132`), and drain-to-empty resets head and tail to zero (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:3933-3946`). The equal-size, mixed-size, prepared-path, and empty-bucket pins are well targeted for those mechanisms (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:10261-10334`, `10336-10437`, `10508-10551`).
docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:39:- **Finding 1 (HIGH)**: CLOSED — `queue_vtime` is restored on both `push_front` branches for the most recent pop/restore pair. Citation: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4023-4028`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4054-4101`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4142-4149`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4177-4189`. `cos_queue_pop_front()` now snapshots pre-pop head/tail before `queue_vtime += bytes`; active-bucket restore subtracts the pushed item's bytes and reverses the pop-time head advance, while drained-bucket restore subtracts the same bytes and reinstates the matching snapshot. An intervening `cos_queue_push_back()` also clears `last_pop_snapshot`, so stale head/tail state is not replayed.
docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:45:- **Finding 4 (MEDIUM)**: CLOSED — I do not see a multi-threaded queue-runtime race or stale-snapshot replay in the current pop→push_back→push_front sequencing. Citation: `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4023-4028`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types.rs:1156-1159`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types.rs:1181-1186`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker.rs:2012-2016`. `cos_queue_push_back()` invalidates the snapshot before any fresh enqueue can reuse it, and the queue runtime is owner-worker single-writer, so this is a logical ordering question rather than a shared-memory race.

docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:51:- **NEW-1 (MEDIUM)**: Multi-pop rollback still only exactly restores the most recently drained bucket; earlier drained buckets in the same LIFO restore fall back to `max(tail, queue_vtime) + bytes` and can overshoot their pre-pop finish. docs/pr/785-phase3/codex-review.md:59:- **NEW-1 (MEDIUM)**: CLOSED — 4-pop/4-pushfront rollback is round-trip neutral. `CoSQueuePopSnapshot` stores bucket + pre-pop head/tail (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/types.rs:1016-1026`); `cos_queue_pop_front()` pushes one snapshot per pop and mutates `queue_vtime`, head/active-set, and bucket bytes (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4166-4239`, `userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:3924-3948`), while `cos_queue_push_front()` rewinds `queue_vtime`, restores drained buckets from the matching LIFO snapshot or reverses the active-bucket head advance, and re-adds bytes/active state (`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/tx.rs:4047-4163`). docs/issues/issue-history.md:11087:## #705 — SFQ bucket collision + per-flow admission cap forces colliding flows into cwnd-collapse regime [CLOSED] (closed 2026-04-17)
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11091:The per-flow admission cap introduced in PR #692 (`cos_queue_flow_share_limit`) divides the exact queue's buffer by `active_flow_buckets`. Under SFQ bucket collision, two flows sharing a bucket get a combined admission slot equal to *one* flow's worth — effectively halving each colliding flow's admission budget. Combined with the small absolute buffer size (~125 KB on the 1g exact queue) and a 16-flow workload, the per-bucket budget drops to ~5–6 packets. That's below TCP's fast-retransmit threshold (3 dupacks), so single-packet drops force RTO → cwnd reset to 1 MSS → the cwnd-collapse oscillation observed in #704.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11096:- 16 iperf3 flows distributed over 64 SFQ buckets via hashed 5-tuple
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11097:- Birthday paradox expected collisions: `16 × 15 / (2 × 64) ≈ 1.88` colliding pairs, so typically 2–4 flows share buckets
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11098:- `active_flow_buckets` = 14 (2 collisions out of 16 flows land in 14 buckets)
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11099:- per-bucket cap = `buffer / active_flow_buckets` = 125 KB / 14 ≈ **9 KB** = **6 MSS (1500 B)**
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11100:- For flows that collide, their *effective* per-flow admission cap is *half* the bucket cap = ~3 MSS
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11104:TCP cubic fast-retransmit fires on 3 dupacks. With 6 packets in flight, a single drop produces at most 2 dupacks before the window is exhausted. That forces an RTO (~200 ms in the cluster) instead of fast-recovery. RTO resets cwnd to 1 MSS. Next round: cwnd ramps from 1, probes past the bucket cap on iteration, single drop, RTO again. That's exactly the observed state on the 11 collapsed flows in #704 — `max_cwnd` 10–40 KB is where cwnd oscillates between "just below bucket cap" and "1 MSS".
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11110:### Option A: grow bucket count (narrowest slice)
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11112:Raise `COS_FLOW_FAIR_BUCKETS` from 64 to 256 or 1024. Birthday-paradox collision rate drops quadratically:
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11114:- 64 buckets, 16 flows: ~88% chance ≥1 collision
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11115:- 256 buckets, 16 flows: ~37% chance ≥1 collision
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11116:- 1024 buckets, 16 flows: ~11% chance ≥1 collision
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11118:Cost: per-queue `flow_bucket_bytes: [u64; N]` (N × 8 B) and `flow_bucket_items: [VecDeque; N]` (N × 24 B + allocated backing storage). At N=1024: 32 KB per queue before allocation. Per-interface with ~8 queues × 4 workers = 1 MB of fixed overhead. Acceptable on modern systems.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11120:### Option B: separate admission cap from bucket count
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11122:The admission cap is there to prevent one flow from hogging the buffer. The SFQ bucket count is there to provide round-robin dequeue fairness. They don't need to share the same denominator. Compute admission cap from a tracked *distinct flow count* (hash-set or approximate-count data structure) rather than `active_flow_buckets`. A colliding pair still gets 2× cap instead of 1× cap.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11126:Replace hashed-bucket SFQ with a flow table keyed on 5-tuple. Each flow gets its own tracking state. Expensive on insert/lookup but eliminates collision entirely. Only worth it if Option A still shows collisions at the scales we care about (> 256 flows/queue, which isn't the current workload).
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11145:- 5 flows run with healthy cwnd (~100 KB), retrans 256–476 per 30 s
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11187:The 1g exact queue's buffer (125 KB = `buffer-size 125k` in config, floored at `COS_MIN_BURST_BYTES = 96 KB`) is sized for single-flow BDP at the aggregate rate. For multi-flow workloads at high parallelism the per-flow BDP share is too small for TCP to stay out of RTO recovery.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11197:TCP cubic / BBR typically want buffer ≥ 2× BDP for steady-state throughput. At 1× BDP, any microburst overflows. Combined with SFQ bucket-cap dividing admission further (#705), each flow's admissible window is well below its transport-layer BDP.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11201:The buffer undersize alone wouldn't be fatal — with enough slack, the SFQ bucket cap and the redirect jitter would be absorbed. At 1× BDP:
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11203:- Any microburst above 9 KB in one flow bucket → tail-drop
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11220:Track `active_flow_buckets` (already tracked for admission) and scale effective buffer as `max(buffer_bytes, active_flows × per_flow_min_depth)`. docs/issues/issue-history.md:11224:Current design conflates them. An admission check on a 9 KB bucket cap with a 125 KB physical buffer means the queue is usually 80%+ empty at the dequeue side. Decouple: keep the physical VecDeque backing large (e.g. 2× BDP at peak aggregate rate), but set per-flow admission based on observed RTT × fair-share rate.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11235:The CoS shaper paces the **dequeue** side of the queue (root and per-queue token buckets). There is no pacing at the **enqueue** side. TCP senders on the host side of the firewall send at cwnd-rate in bursts — a cwnd worth of packets goes out back-to-back, then the sender waits for acks. Those bursts land in the CoS queue as a burst, not as a paced stream. Under multi-flow concurrency this produces microburst peaks that overflow per-flow admission caps (#705) and the physical buffer (#707) even when the steady-state aggregate is well under rate.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11239:Token-bucket shapers smooth over *windows*. A queue with `transmit-rate 1g` and `buffer-size 125k` will happily let 125 KB arrive in 1 µs and then release it at 1 Gbps over 1 ms. That's fine for one sender but breaks multi-flow fairness:
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11256:### Option A: token-bucket pacing on enqueue
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11258:Before `cos_queue_push_back` / admission check, run the packet through a token-bucket sized to the flow's fair-share rate. If tokens < packet_size, block the packet (synchronous wait) or defer (async, via timer wheel). Same token-bucket primitive as the existing shaper, applied on the other side.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11260:Problems: can't block in userspace RX path — backpressure would be needed. And "flow's fair-share rate" isn't known a priori; would need estimation or a per-flow token bucket with a quasi-static cap.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11262:### Option B: rate-limited enqueue at the per-bucket level
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11264:Each SFQ bucket gets a token bucket sized to `queue_rate / bucket_count`. Packets can be enqueued up to the bucket's token budget; excess packets get dropped or deferred. Approximates per-flow pacing without needing per-flow state.

docs/issues/issue-history.md:11375:## #711 — SFQ 64 buckets is too small — bucket collision probability dominates at 16+ flows [CLOSED] (closed 2026-04-17)
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11379:The current low-rate exact SFQ design uses 64 hashed buckets to approximate per-flow fair queuing. The round-robin dequeue advances bucket-by-bucket, and the per-flow admission cap divides the buffer by `active_flow_buckets`. Two flows that hash to the same bucket share that bucket's dequeue slot *and* its admission cap. SFQ's promise is per-flow fairness; at 64 buckets with realistic hash collision rates, we deliver per-BUCKET fairness, which is not quite the same thing.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11383:Birthday paradox for N flows into B buckets, probability of ≥1 collision:
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11401:"Per-flow fair" means: on a backlogged queue, each flow gets equal share of the output rate. SFQ bucketing trades this off for constant-time lookup — you look up the bucket by hash, not by tracking distinct flows. If the hash is large enough, collisions are rare and the approximation is good. 64 buckets is fine for ≤8 flows and broken for 16+.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11407:### Option A: grow bucket count
docs/issues/issue-history.md:11593:Flow buckets regularly exceed 24 KB (TCP bursts past fair share during recovery), triggering per-flow admission drops. #718's aggregate threshold never fires because the aggregate stays at ~30% utilisation while per-flow buckets are hitting their cap.

docs/issues/issue-history.md:13892:## #837 — Slice C-a: full HOL-finish cross-binding MQFQ with shared vtime + per-bucket state machine [OPEN]
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13896:#836 proposed promoting \`flow_bucket_head_finish_bytes\` + \`flow_bucket_tail_finish_bytes\` from per-binding to per-lease shared atomic arrays, while keeping \`queue_vtime\` per-binding. Full review at \`docs/pr/836-shared-flow-vtime/codex-plan-review.md\`.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13901:2. **Head-lift race on concurrent same-bucket enqueue** — two bindings enqueuing on one bucket can overwrite the correct HOL-finish with the wrong value when their \`queue_vtime\`s differ.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13904:5. **No global-idle detection** — monotonic head-lift catches stale-low but not stale-high. An idle-for-hours bucket returns with a frozen high finish time; next enqueue anchors too far ahead.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13905:6. **Double-service on same bucket** — two bindings can both pick the globally-minimum-head bucket on one RR pass, violating the Phase 3 equal-depth interleaving invariant.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13910:2. **Per-bucket \`active_count\`** (\`[AtomicU16; COS_FLOW_FAIR_BUCKETS]\` or equivalent). Increment on local 0→N enqueue transitions, decrement on local N→0 dequeue transitions. Enables global-idle detection.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13912:4. **Per-bucket dequeue claim/epoch** so only one binding services a bucket per RR pass. Claim acquired pre-selection, released post-commit-or-rollback.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13914:6. **Correct head-lift on idle→active transition**: only ONE binding wins the transition (via CAS on active_count 0→1); that binding sets \`head = tail = max(queue_vtime_shared, old_tail) + bytes\`. Losers of the CAS fall through to the normal active-bucket enqueue path (\`tail += bytes\`) against the now-installed head.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13920:- At least 40 new unit tests including: same-bucket A-pop/B-pop/A-rollback, globally-idle re-entry with stale-high head, two-bindings-select-same-bucket race, late-binding promotion with live shared state, concurrent-enqueue tail CAS loop under \`max(old, qv) + bytes\` discipline.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13924:- Very easy to regress throughput if atomic contention dominates. #833 and #834 both regressed on shared_exact changes. The per-bucket state machine adds 2+ atomics per packet dispatch.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13946:The root issue: **HOL-finish-time is not a commutative quantity**. It's a per-packet timestamp, changes non-additively on every dequeue (head advances to the NEW HOL packet's finish), and rollback requires snapshot state rather than arithmetic reversal. Sharing it across bindings safely requires a per-bucket ownership state machine + shared virtual-time clock + snapshot rollback — a very large surface (tracked in #837).
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13958:- \`period_bytes_per_flow: Box<[CachePaddedAtomicU64; N]>\` — bytes dispatched per flow hash bucket this window.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13964:- **Dequeue**: after each packet dispatch, \`fetch_add(bytes, Relaxed)\` on \`period_bytes_per_flow[bucket]\` and \`period_bytes_total\`.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:13966:- **Selection gating**: before picking bucket \`b\` in \`cos_queue_min_finish_bucket\`, read \`period_bytes_per_flow[b]\` and \`period_bytes_total\`. Compute \`fair_share = period_bytes_total / active_bucket_count\` (counted via iteration or a cached counter). If \`period_bytes_per_flow[b] > fair_share × (1 + epsilon)\`, **skip this bucket in THIS pass** (penalty = one RR cycle). docs/issues/issue-history.md:15848:Direct-mapped caches were abandoned in hardware decades ago because of **Cache Thrashing**. In the '100E100M' scenario, if an Elephant flow and a Mouse flow happen to hash to the same bucket (which is almost guaranteed by the Birthday Paradox with only 4096 buckets), they will unconditionally evict each other on every single packet. 
docs/issues/issue-history.md:15853:Implement a **4-way or 8-way Set Associative Cache**. Use a small array of entries per bucket and apply an LRU (Least Recently Used) or Random replacement policy. Alternatively, use a modern lock-free hash map structure (like a sharded `SwissTable`). Never use a 1-way direct-mapped cache for flow state.

docs/issues/issue-history.md:19857:\`userspace-dp/src/afxdp/worker/mod.rs:1934-1956\` in Interrupt mode:
docs/issues/issue-history.md:19874:\`IDLE_SPIN_ITERS = 256\` (afxdp/mod.rs:227). The latency-hedge rationale is sound (back-to-back TCP ACKs collapse cwnd if the worker blocks immediately on the first empty poll). The problem is the **unit cost** of an empty iteration:
docs/issues/issue-history.md:19876:Each iteration calls \`poll_binding(idx, …)\` for every binding (worker/mod.rs:1247-1287). With ~18 bindings × ~30-50ns per ring-peek pair, one empty iter ≈ **1-2µs**, not 50-100ns. So 256 iters ≈ **256-512µs of CPU hedge** per spin-out cycle. At any aggregate rate above ~2 kpps (inter-packet gap < 500µs), workers stay inside the spin window indefinitely and never reach \`poll(2)\`.
docs/issues/issue-history.md:19927:The `.load()` call itself goes through `arc_swap::HybridStrategy::load` which does atomic load + thread-local debt-list bookkeeping. The cost per call is ~30-80ns. With 12 fields × 256 spin iterations × 6 workers, that's ~92K-245K loads per spin cycle aggregate — 2.7-19µs of cumulative HybridStrategy::load cost per cycle, scaled across all workers.

docs/issues/pr-history.md:7211:1024 covers the production regime (N ≤ 64 flows/queue) with headroom. Not 4096 or higher — the per-queue memory overhead of `[VecDeque; N]` inline headers grows linearly and the gains beyond 1024 stop mattering for realistic flow counts.
docs/issues/pr-history.md:7215:**Bucket ID width: u16.** 1024 buckets need 10 bits. `u8` (the prior return type of `exact_cos_flow_bucket`) would have silently truncated the hash to 8 bits — giving the widened mask no actual work to do. u16 is the minimum that exposes the full 10-bit bucket space; u32 would waste cache.
docs/issues/pr-history.md:7219:**Invariant unchanged.** The callers in `cos_queue_push_*` / `cos_queue_pop_front` already gate on "bucket transitioned empty → non-empty" before pushing, and on "bucket still non-empty" before re-enqueueing the RR cursor after dequeue. The ring itself does not re-validate on the hot path. New ring-invariant unit tests pin this contract (no-duplicates, wrap-around, capacity edges).
docs/issues/pr-history.md:7231:Within noise, slightly faster if anything. The fixed ring avoids the `VecDeque<u8>` heap indirection on push/pop; the bucket-count grow itself doesn't affect per-packet cost (same O(1) ops, same cache behavior for the small active-bucket set actually in use).
docs/issues/pr-history.md:7288:2. **Flow-aware aggregate cap** matching the per-flow clamp's denominator. Per-flow clamp already reasoned about *prospective* active flows (current + 1 when the target bucket is empty). Aggregate cap was keyed off current active count, so at the new-flow boundary the per-flow gate admitted the first packet while the aggregate gate rejected it. Helper `cos_flow_aware_buffer_limit(queue, flow_bucket)` now uses the same prospective-active formula, driven from a single `flow_bucket` computed once per admission.
docs/issues/pr-history.md:7294:- One `flow_bucket` computation per admission (already present, reordered earlier).
docs/issues/pr-history.md:7383:`cos_flow_aware_buffer_limit()` after #716 scales the aggregate admission cap with `prospective_active × COS_FLOW_FAIR_MIN_SHARE_BYTES`. With the #711 bucket grow this reaches `1024 × 24 KB ≈ 24 MB` at max. On a 1 Gbps queue that is `~190 ms` of queue residence — far outside the scheduler's predictable regime. Flagged in #716 review; explicitly deferred because clamping queueing delay is a behaviour choice, not a bug fix.

docs/issues/pr-history.md:15320:## PR #1075 — Cold Start 1: MAX_PENDING_NEIGH 64→4096 + retry_pending_neigh O(N²)→O(N) [MERGED] (merged 2026-05-01)
docs/issues/pr-history.md:15330:### Item 1: buffer cap 64 → 4096
docs/issues/pr-history.md:15336:The previous `retry_pending_neigh` body in `afxdp/neighbor_dispatch.rs` did `binding.pending_neigh.remove(i)` inside a while-i-loop. `VecDeque::remove` is O(n) per call, so the sweep was O(n²) in queue depth. With the cap bumped to 4096 the quadratic cost would be a real fairness hazard.
docs/issues/pr-history.md:15362:## PR #1076 — Fairness 1: COS_FLOW_FAIR_BUCKETS 1024 → 4096 [MERGED] (merged 2026-05-01)
docs/issues/pr-history.md:15368:GEMINI-NEXT.md Section 2 ("100E100M Fairness Solution") item 4: bucket-collision fix.
docs/issues/pr-history.md:15370:The 1024-bucket SFQ size was sized in #711 for "production-regime flow count N ≤ 64 per queue". Real 100E100M workloads (100 Elephant + 100 Mouse flows per CoS class) push 200+ concurrent flows per queue, where birthday-paradox collision probability approaches **99%**. Two flows colliding into the same bucket compete for one SFQ dequeue slot and one admission-cap slice (#705), which silently destroys fairness even when MQFQ ordering is correct.

docs/issues/pr-history.md:18818:Adds an explicit \`surplus-sharing\` boolean config flag on CoS schedulers that, when set on a \`transmit-rate <r> exact\` queue, lifts the surplus-phase skip in \`select_cos_surplus_batch\` so the queue can draw from root surplus tokens once its own bucket is empty. Default = false (preserves Junos \`transmit-rate exact\` hard-cap semantics for every existing operator).
docs/issues/pr-history.md:18822:Concrete scenario: an \`iperf-a 1 Gb/s exact\` queue on a 10 Gb/s interface. Today it stays at 1 Gb/s even when the other 9 Gb/s of root capacity is idle. With \`surplus-sharing\` opted in, it can burst into the spare bandwidth. Validated on the loss userspace cluster: iperf-a 967 Mbps without flag → **2.57 Gbps with flag** (alone), → 2.27 Gbps with iperf-b at 9 Gb/s concurrent (both classes coexist).
docs/issues/pr-history.md:18837:1. **Park-on-starvation race (§4.5)**: An exact queue whose \`queue.tokens < head_len\` was parked by the exact-guarantee selector BEFORE the surplus selector ran. Once parked, surplus skipped it via \`!queue.runnable\`. The fix adds a \`if queue.surplus_sharing { continue; }\` branch BEFORE \`park_cos_queue\` so the queue stays runnable. The \`drain_park_queue_tokens\` diagnostic counter still increments (the bucket DID starve).

docs/pr/816-step1-rerun/codex-plan-review.md:56:**Flaw:** "Copy #812 §11.3 verbatim" is false. The accepted D3 statistic in #812 is `1{tail} * 1{tx_pause > 0}`. This plan deletes the `tx_pause` term and still runs the result through the same `p_v <= 0.05`, `k_v >= 2`, and hypothesis-branch machinery. That is no longer a D3 test; it is a generic rare-tail detector confounded by count, C-like stalls, and anything else that can touch buckets 14-15.
docs/pr/816-step1-rerun/codex-plan-review.md:70:**Flaw:** I11 is derived from the wrong model and the wrong object. `T_D1,b` and `T_D2,b` are ratios/products of multinomial bucket masses over a fixed block count; they are not raw Poisson arrivals, and the permutation test operates on block-to-block variation, not on a single bucket's counting error at an invented `p = 0.05`.
docs/pr/816-step1-rerun/codex-plan-review.md:74:**Mitigation:** Redefine I11 in terms of the actual classifier objects. docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:20:  This is a **critical math error**. In Prometheus, a histogram metric family is not a single series; it generates a separate series for *each bucket* (labeled by `le`).
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:21:  * Under Plan v2, the `ns_bucket_v2` metric generates: `128 slots × 8 workers × 80 buckets = 81,920` time-series.
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:26:  * **Linear Band**: `[0, 512) ns` split into 32 buckets of 16-ns stride. (32 buckets).
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:27:  * **Exponential Band**: `[512, 2^24) ns` split into 15 power-of-two buckets (`[512, 1024)`, `[1024, 2048)`, ..., `[2^23, 2^24)`). (15 buckets).
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:28:  * **Saturate Band**: `ns ≥ 2^24` (1 bucket).
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:30:  * **Relative Error Verification**: A sample at 600 ns landing in the `[512, 1024)` bucket has a worst-case error of `(1024-512)/768 = 67%` (1.67× error), which easily satisfies the "≤2× error" target. 
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:31:  * **Impact**: Halving the bucket count from 80 to 48 reduces Prometheus metric cardinality by **40%** and speeds up `histogram_quantile()` computation significantly, with zero loss in resolution in the critical `50-150 ns` range.
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:41:  * **Operational Impact**: With sparse serialization, wire footprint drops from 82 KB/worker to **~8 KB/worker** (a 90% bandwidth reduction!). More importantly, we can safely increase the maximum Rust slot map capacity to **256 or 512** with *zero* wire overhead, completely eliminating the lifetime overflow risk.
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:49:* **Upgrade Safety**: Verified. The `cold_path_layout_version = 2` u32 tag safely prevents older Go control planes from misinterpreting the new 80-bucket (or 48-bucket) arrays as v1.
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:66:  This is a **critical performance risk**. `lookup_slot` performs a `FastMap` (hashmap) lookup *on the hot path*. Under standard 1-in-256 sampling, this cost is amortized. 
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:77:* **Aggregate vs. Per-Zone-Pair**: Committing strictly to per-zone-pair publication and removing the mixed "aggregate row" in the dataplane is architecturally correct. Pre-aggregating in the dataplane corrupts the distribution. Operators should perform aggregate calculations (e.g., p50 across all zone pairs) in PromQL by summing cumulative buckets.
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:80:* **Hard-Refuse Verdict**: Hard-refuse is acceptable only if the slot capacity is sufficiently high (e.g., 256 or 512). If slot count is capped at 128 without slot reuse, dynamic policies will inevitably trigger permanent metrics blackout for new zones over a long daemon uptime.
docs/pr/1635-cold-path-hist-redesign/agy-plan-r1.md:81:  * Implementing **Sparse Serialization** (discussed in 1.2) unlocks a larger slot limit (256/512) with zero wire penalty.

docs/pr/819-step2-discriminator-design/plan.md:219:**Definition: "T_D1-elevated blocks".** A 5-s block `b` is "T_D1-elevated" if its `T_D1,b` value (the bucket-3-to-6 mass fraction per #816 plan §4.2 / `step1-histogram-classify.py:159-163`) is in the **top quartile** of the 12 blocks in the cell's capture, i.e. `T_D1,b ≥ percentile(T_D1, 75)`. Concretely: rank the 12 block values, take the top 3 (12 ÷ 4 = 3 rounded). Reference: `evidence/with-cos/<cell>/hist-blocks.jsonl` lines 1-12, field `shape[3]+shape[4]+shape[5]+shape[6]`. Used by T1, T2, T4 below for "during T_D1-elevated blocks" and by T3 for the inconclusive-band re-bin.
docs/pr/819-step2-discriminator-design/plan.md:221:- **T3 — M3 IN via P1:** `Spearman(T_D1,b, off_cpu_time_buckets_3to6_b) ≥ 0.8` (computed across all 12 blocks) **AND** `sum_over_blocks(off_cpu_time_buckets_3to6) / 60s ≥ 1%`. **T3 OUT:** `ρ ≤ 0.3` OR `total_off_cpu_3to6 / 60s < 1%`. **T3 INCONCLUSIVE:** `0.3 < ρ < 0.8`. Justification: §7.1.
docs/pr/819-step2-discriminator-design/plan.md:222:- **T1 — M1 IN via P3 (HIGH-2 PARTIAL Round-3 — pre-registered, no post-hoc band):** `Δ(retry_counter)/block ≥ 1000 events` during T_D1-elevated blocks (top 3 blocks per §4.1 definition) **AND** `mean(sendto_kick_latency) ≥ 4 µs` (lower edge of bucket 3). **T1 OUT:** `Δ(retry_counter)/block < 100 events on every block` AND `mean(sendto_kick_latency) < 2 µs across all blocks` (bucket ≤ 1, below where D1 lives). **T1 INCONCLUSIVE:** anything between (e.g. retry counter in 100–1000/block range, or mean kick latency in 2–4 µs band). Pre-registered before P3 captures; the "calibration band set after first capture" clause from Round 2 is withdrawn — the IN/OUT/INCONCLUSIVE bands are fixed thresholds.

docs/pr/797-d3/codex-review.md:45:The code applies weights on startup (`pkg/daemon/rss_indirection.go:161-178`) but skips for `workers == 1` and `workers >= queues` (`pkg/daemon/rss_indirection.go:106-109`, `193-205`), and the only call site is the startup path (`pkg/daemon/linksetup.go:100-104`). docs/pr/797-d3/codex-review.md:113:But daemon interactive mode still bypasses that path. In interactive mode the daemon creates a local CLI (`pkg/daemon/daemon.go:1076-1079`); CLI commits call `c.applyToDataplane(compiled)` directly (`pkg/cli/cli_config.go:170-239`), and `applyToDataplane()` compiles the dataplane but never calls `d.applyConfig()` or `reapplyRSSIndirection()` (`pkg/cli/cli.go:1407-1434`; `reapplyRSSIndirection` not found under `pkg/cli`). So a live `set system dataplane workers N` committed from the in-process CLI still skips the D3 reapply.
docs/pr/797-d3/codex-review.md:139:H2: CLOSED — local CLI bare `commit`, `commit comment`, and `commit confirmed N` all route through `c.commitApply(compiled)` (`pkg/cli/cli_config.go:185-251`), `commitApply()` prefers `applyConfigFn` (`pkg/cli/cli_config.go:12-32`), and the daemon wires `d.applyConfig` into the in-process CLI (`pkg/daemon/daemon.go:1082-1090`).      1	//! #1651 Path B3: dead-host negative neighbor cache.
     2	//!
     3	//! A per-binding, short-TTL cache of `(egress_ifindex, next_hop)` keys that
     4	//! failed to resolve within `PENDING_NEIGH_TIMEOUT`. While a dst is present,
     5	//! un-expired, and still-unresolved, new `MissingNeighbor` packets to it
     6	//! fast-fail (recycle) at the buffer site instead of each consuming a
     7	//! `pending_neigh` slot for the full timeout window.
     8	//!
     9	//! This is the AGY-r1 HIGH starvation defense from the reopened-#1651
    10	//! research: a dead-host SYN storm can otherwise saturate the bounded
    11	//! `pending_neigh` queue (cap `MAX_PENDING_NEIGH`, 800 ms hold each) and
    12	//! starve LIVE cold connects at the full-queue gate.
    13	//!
    14	//! ## Invalidation
    15	//! - **RTM_NEWNEIGH (host recovered):** lazy resolved-neighbor-wins. The
    16	//!   caller checks `forwarding.neighbors` then `dynamic_neighbors` BEFORE
    17	//!   honoring a negative entry; on a resolved hit it calls
    18	//!   [`neg_neigh_evict`] and forwards normally. The shared netlink monitor
    19	//!   thread populates `dynamic_neighbors`, so a recovered host that receives
    20	//!   traffic is evicted on its very next packet — no monitor→per-binding
    21	//!   coupling needed.
    22	//! - **TTL:** [`neg_neigh_active`] evicts on access once the entry is older
    23	//!   than `NEG_NEIGH_TTL_NS`.
    24	//!
    25	//! ## Placement
    26	//! Per-binding (mirrors `pending_neigh`). Touched ONLY by the owning worker
    27	//! thread (both `poll_descriptor` and `retry_pending_neigh` run on it), so no
    28	//! `Arc`/`Mutex`/cross-core sync — consistent with the per-queue AF_XDP model.
    29	
    30	use super::types::FastMap;
    31	use super::{MAX_NEG_NEIGH_CACHE, NEG_NEIGH_TTL_NS};
    32	use std::net::IpAddr;
    33	
    34	/// Negative-cache map type: key `(egress_ifindex, next_hop)`, value =
    35	/// insertion `now_ns`.
    36	pub(super) type NegNeighCache = FastMap<(i32, IpAddr), u64>;
    37	
    38	/// Returns true if `key` is currently negatively cached (present AND
    39	/// un-expired). Expired entries are evicted on access (lazy TTL).
    40	///
    41	/// Does NOT consult the neighbor maps — the caller must check
    42	/// `forwarding.neighbors` / `dynamic_neighbors` FIRST so a resolved dst wins
    43	/// (RTM_NEWNEIGH eviction). This keeps the function pure w.r.t. the neighbor
    44	/// maps and trivially testable.
    45	pub(super) fn neg_neigh_active(cache: &mut NegNeighCache, key: &(i32, IpAddr), now_ns: u64) -> bool {
    46	    match cache.get(key) {
    47	        Some(&inserted) if now_ns.saturating_sub(inserted) < NEG_NEIGH_TTL_NS => true,
    48	        Some(_) => {
    49	            // Expired — evict on access so the map self-prunes.
    50	            cache.remove(key);
    51	            false
    52	        }
    53	        None => false,
    54	    }
    55	}
    56	
    57	/// Record a dead-host drop at `now_ns`. Bounded by `MAX_NEG_NEIGH_CACHE`: on
    58	/// overflow (and only when inserting a genuinely new key) the map is cleared
    59	/// wholesale. `clear()` retains capacity, so this is allocation-free.
    60	pub(super) fn neg_neigh_record(cache: &mut NegNeighCache, key: (i32, IpAddr), now_ns: u64) {
    61	    if cache.len() >= MAX_NEG_NEIGH_CACHE && !cache.contains_key(&key) {
    62	        cache.clear();
    63	    }
    64	    cache.insert(key, now_ns);
    65	}
    66	
    67	/// Explicit eviction (resolved-neighbor-wins). Idempotent.
    68	pub(super) fn neg_neigh_evict(cache: &mut NegNeighCache, key: &(i32, IpAddr)) {
    69	    cache.remove(key);
    70	}
    71	
    72	/// The full dead-host gate decision used at the `MissingNeighbor` handler.
    73	///
    74	/// `is_resolved` is the caller-supplied resolved-neighbor probe (static
    75	/// `forwarding.neighbors` THEN `dynamic_neighbors`, in that order — the
    76	/// closure encapsulates the lookup so this helper stays decoupled from the
    77	/// concrete map types and is unit-testable in isolation).
    78	///
    79	/// Semantics (resolved-neighbor-wins, then TTL):
    80	/// - If the dst is now resolved, any stale negative entry is evicted and the
    81	///   gate returns `false` (proceed to normal forwarding). This is the
    82	///   RTM_NEWNEIGH invalidation path.
    83	/// - Else, if the dst is negatively cached + un-expired, return `true`
    84	///   (fast-fail: caller recycles the frame without buffering / probing /
    85	///   seeding a session).
    86	/// - Else return `false` (proceed: first cold connect for this dst, or the
    87	///   negative entry has expired).
    88	///
    89	/// Returns `true` ⇒ the caller must fast-fail this packet.
    90	pub(super) fn neg_neigh_gate<F: FnOnce() -> bool>(
    91	    cache: &mut NegNeighCache,
    92	    key: &(i32, IpAddr),
    93	    now_ns: u64,
    94	    is_resolved: F,
    95	) -> bool {
    96	    if is_resolved() {
    97	        neg_neigh_evict(cache, key);
    98	        false
    99	    } else {
   100	        neg_neigh_active(cache, key, now_ns)
   101	    }
   102	}
   103	
   104	#[cfg(test)]
   105	mod tests {
   106	    use super::*;
   107	    use crate::afxdp::{MAX_NEG_NEIGH_CACHE, NEG_NEIGH_TTL_NS};
   108	    use std::net::Ipv4Addr;
   109	
   110	    fn key(last: u8) -> (i32, IpAddr) {
   111	        (14, IpAddr::V4(Ipv4Addr::new(172, 16, 80, last)))
   112	    }
   113	
   114	    #[test]
   115	    fn record_then_active_within_ttl() {
   116	        let mut c = NegNeighCache::default();
   117	        neg_neigh_record(&mut c, key(137), 1_000);
   118	        assert!(neg_neigh_active(&mut c, &key(137), 1_000));
   119	        // Just under TTL: still active.
   120	        assert!(neg_neigh_active(
   121	            &mut c,
   122	            &key(137),
   123	            1_000 + NEG_NEIGH_TTL_NS - 1
   124	        ));
   125	    }
   126	
   127	    #[test]
   128	    fn expires_at_ttl_boundary_and_evicts_on_access() {
   129	        let mut c = NegNeighCache::default();
   130	        neg_neigh_record(&mut c, key(137), 1_000);
   131	        // Exactly TTL elapsed (now - inserted == TTL) is NOT active (< TTL).
   132	        assert!(!neg_neigh_active(&mut c, &key(137), 1_000 + NEG_NEIGH_TTL_NS));
   133	        // The expired entry was evicted on access.
   134	        assert!(!c.contains_key(&key(137)));
   135	    }
   136	
   137	    #[test]
   138	    fn absent_key_is_not_active() {
   139	        let mut c = NegNeighCache::default();

   141	    }
   142	
   143	    #[test]
   144	    fn evict_is_idempotent() {
   145	        let mut c = NegNeighCache::default();
   146	        neg_neigh_record(&mut c, key(137), 1_000);
   147	        neg_neigh_evict(&mut c, &key(137));
   148	        assert!(!neg_neigh_active(&mut c, &key(137), 1_000));
   149	        // Second evict on an already-absent key is a no-op, no panic.
   150	        neg_neigh_evict(&mut c, &key(137));
   151	        assert!(!c.contains_key(&key(137)));
   152	    }
   153	
   154	    #[test]

   156	        // Simulates the RTM_NEWNEIGH path: a dead host is negatively cached,
   157	        // then resolves (caller evicts on the resolved-wins check). The same
   158	        // key must no longer fast-fail.

   161	        assert!(neg_neigh_active(&mut c, &key(137), 1_500));
   162	        // Host came back → caller evicts.
   163	        neg_neigh_evict(&mut c, &key(137));

   165	    }
